common.applies_to: Established bush rose (Hybrid Tea, Floribunda, provisional Grandiflora); dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: The two sources that put a number on "pencil thickness" disagree (about 6 mm versus 10 mm, C-1), so Pip uses no number. Why canes become weak is thinly evidenced; one source links congestion to weak growth, and one links old age to it (AF-2, Low). No source describes weak canes as arching or flopping, so that isn't used as a sign (U-2).

content.look_for: Let's look for weak canes — thinner than a pencil, twiggy or unproductive — and at whether the middle of the bush is crowded.

criteria.text: A cane thinner than about a pencil is a candidate weak cane. No number is used.
Twiggy or unproductive growth, with thin tips rather than full, lush canes.
Crowded: the bush is densely packed, especially at ground level, rather than open in the middle.
A thin cane with brown or reddish thorns may be this season's new growth rather than a weak cane.

content.photo_limit: Without a size reference, thickness can't be judged from a photo — hold a coin or pencil beside the cane. No photo can rule out crowding at the back of the bush.
content.confirm_question: Check the cane against a pencil, and look at the middle of the bush from more than one side. Is it weak, or is the bush crowded?
content.not_sure_guidance: Take a photo with a coin or pencil beside the cane, or look at the middle from another side, then check again.
content.any_more_question: Can you see any more weak canes?
